title: Minimal free model over a local ring
statement: Let $(R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$ be a local ring and let $K\in D(R)$ [def-weil-abstract-derived-category] be pseudo-coherent [def-pc-ring-pseudo-coherent-complex], that is, isomorphic in $D(R)$ to a bounded-above complex of finite free $R$-modules. Put $d_i=\dim_\kappa H^i(K\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}\kappa)$. If the $d_i$ are finite and vanish for all sufficiently large $i$, then $K$ is represented by a bounded-above complex of finite free $R$-modules whose term in degree $i$ is $R^{\oplus d_i}$. Such a complex is unique up to isomorphism of complexes.

proof.text: Choose an integer $b$ with $d_i=0$ for $i>b$. Every complex of $\kappa$-vector spaces is quasi-isomorphic to the complex of its cohomology spaces with zero differential (choose complements of the boundaries in the cycles and of the cycles in the terms). Hence $K\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}\kappa$ is represented in $D(\kappa)$ by the complex $E^\bullet$ with $E^i=\kappa^{\oplus d_i}$ and zero differentials; its terms are finite free because the $d_i$ are finite, and it is bounded above because $E^i=0$ for $i>b$.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma 15.75.7, proof: splitting complexes over a field

proof.text: Apply [lem-sc-pseudo-coherent-lift-stably-free-complex] with $I=\mathfrak m$: every element of $1+\mathfrak m$ is a unit of the local ring $R$, $K$ is pseudo-coherent, and $E^\bullet$ is a bounded-above complex of finite free (in particular finite stably free) $\kappa$-modules representing $K\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}\kappa$. It gives a bounded-above complex $P^\bullet$ of finite free $R$-modules representing $K$ in $D(R)$ with an isomorphism of complexes $P^\bullet\otimes_R\kappa\cong E^\bullet$.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma 15.75.7, proof: apply Lemma 15.75.6 (Tag 0BCB)

proof.text: For each $i$, $P^i\otimes_R\kappa\cong E^i=\kappa^{\oplus d_i}$, and a finite free module $R^{\oplus n}$ over the local ring $R$ has $R^{\oplus n}\otimes_R\kappa=\kappa^{\oplus n}$, so $n=d_i$ and $P^i\cong R^{\oplus d_i}$. Transporting the differentials along these isomorphisms gives the complex of the statement; it is bounded above since $P^i=0$ for $i>b$.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma 15.75.7, displayed conclusion

proof.text: For uniqueness, let $F^\bullet$ and $G^\bullet$ be bounded-above complexes of finite free $R$-modules with $F^i\cong G^i\cong R^{\oplus d_i}$, both isomorphic to $K$ in $D(R)$, and let $\varphi:F^\bullet\to G^\bullet$ be the resulting isomorphism in $D(R)$. Both are bounded-above complexes of projective $R$-modules, so by [lem-pc-ring-derived-map-representative] (in the abelian category of $R$-modules) $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are represented by chain maps $\beta:F^\bullet\to G^\bullet$ and $\alpha:G^\bullet\to F^\bullet$, and since $\alpha\beta$ and $\beta\alpha$ represent the identities, the injectivity in the same lemma makes them chain homotopic to the identities. Thus $\beta$ is a homotopy equivalence, and so is $\beta\otimes_R\kappa:F^\bullet\otimes_R\kappa\to G^\bullet\otimes_R\kappa$; in particular it is a quasi-isomorphism. By [lem-pc-module-bounded-flat-kflat] $F^\bullet$ and $G^\bullet$ are K-flat, so $F^\bullet\otimes_R\kappa$ and $G^\bullet\otimes_R\kappa$ represent $K\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}\kappa$ and $\dim_\kappa H^i(F^\bullet\otimes_R\kappa)=d_i=\dim_\kappa(F^i\otimes_R\kappa)$ for all $i$, likewise for $G^\bullet$. For a complex $C^\bullet$ of finite-dimensional spaces, $\dim H^i(C^\bullet)=\dim C^i-\operatorname{rk}d^i-\operatorname{rk}d^{i-1}$, so both reduced complexes have zero differentials and $\beta^i\otimes 1=H^i(\beta\otimes_R\kappa)$ is an isomorphism for every $i$. By Nakayama's lemma [lem-weil-pbc-nakayama-local-generators] (the image of $\beta^i$ maps onto $G^i/\mathfrak mG^i$), $\beta^i:F^i\to G^i$ is surjective; as $G^i$ is free it splits, $F^i\cong G^i\oplus N$ with $N=\ker\beta^i$ finitely generated, and comparing dimensions over $\kappa$ gives $N/\mathfrak mN=0$, so $N=0$ by the same lemma (applied to the submodule $0\subseteq N$). Hence every $\beta^i$ is an isomorphism and $\beta$ is an isomorphism of complexes.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma 15.75.7, proof: uniqueness of the minimal complex
